title: What is the correct order of database scaling steps, and why is sharding the LAST resort (scale up → optimize queries/indexes → add read replicas → add a cache → CQRS → shard)?
shortTitle: The correct order of database scaling steps, and why sharding is last

s1_definition.profdef: The correct scaling order moves from cheapest and least disruptive to most expensive and most disruptive: optimize queries and indexes, scale up vertically, add read replicas, add a cache, apply CQRS, and only then shard. Sharding is the last resort because it permanently changes the data model, breaks cross-node joins and transactions, and imposes heavy operational cost, so every cheaper option that could remove the bottleneck should be exhausted first.
s1_definition.analogy: When the National Bank branch gets crowded, you first make the clerks work smarter (fix slow processes and indexes), then give them a faster desk (bigger machine), then add read-only clerks for balance enquiries (replicas), then keep a notepad of common answers (cache), then separate the "write" counter from the "read" counter (CQRS). Only when none of that is enough do you split customers across separate branches (sharding), because once you do, answering "total across all branches" and moving money between branches becomes genuinely hard and permanent.
s1_definition.oneliner: Optimize, scale up, replicate, cache, CQRS, then shard — because sharding is a one-way door that breaks joins and transactions.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The correct scaling order moves from cheapest and least disruptive to most expensive and most disruptive: optimize queries and indexes, scale up vertically, add read replicas, add a cache, apply CQRS, and only then shard. Sharding is the last resort because it permanently changes the data model, breaks cross-node joins and transactions, and imposes heavy operational cost, so every cheaper option that could remove the bottleneck should be exhausted first.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** When the National Bank branch gets crowded, you first make the clerks work smarter (fix slow processes and indexes), then give them a faster desk (bigger machine), then add read-only clerks for balance enquiries (replicas), then keep a notepad of common answers (cache), then separate the "write" counter from the "read" counter (CQRS). Only when none of that is enough do you split customers across separate branches (sharding), because once you do, answering "total across all branches" and moving money between branches becomes genuinely hard and permanent.

**One line to remember:** Optimize, scale up, replicate, cache, CQRS, then shard — because sharding is a one-way door that breaks joins and transactions.

sections.s2_technical:
The order matters because each step is dramatically cheaper and less risky than the next, and most systems never need the last step at all.

Step one is optimize queries and indexes. This is free in infrastructure terms and often the entire fix. A missing index turning a scan into a seek can cut a query a thousandfold. If you shard a database that still has unindexed queries, you just multiply an inefficient system.

Step two is scale up vertically — more CPU, memory, and faster NVMe storage on one machine. Modern hardware is enormous; a single node can handle tens of thousands of transactions per second. Vertical scaling requires zero code change and buys significant headroom. Its limit is that there is a biggest machine, and cost rises steeply near the top.

Step three is add read replicas. Most OLTP workloads, especially banking, are read-heavy, so sending reads to replicas frees the primary to handle writes. Replicas are relatively simple: they replay the primary's WAL. The caveat is replication lag, so reads that must be fresh still go to the primary.

Step four is add a cache like Redis. Hot read-mostly data — reference data, hot balances, computed results — served from memory removes huge load from the database and cuts latency to microseconds. The caveat is cache invalidation and staleness, which you manage with TTLs and invalidation on write.

Step five is CQRS, Command Query Responsibility Segregation. You split the write model from one or more read models, each shaped and scaled for its purpose, often with the read side materialized from events. This lets reads and writes scale and evolve independently, and it is a natural stepping stone before sharding.

Step six is sharding, and it is last for concrete reasons. Sharding permanently splits your data across nodes, so joins that used to be a single SQL statement now require application-side fan-out and merge. Transactions that span shards lose simple ACID and require two-phase commit or sagas. Global unique constraints and auto-increment ids no longer work; you need distributed id generation. Choosing a bad shard key creates hot spots that are painful to fix because re-sharding moves enormous amounts of data. Operationally you now run and monitor many nodes, each needing its own backups and replicas. And it is effectively a one-way door — un-sharding is a major project. Because every one of the earlier steps is cheaper, reversible, and often sufficient, you exhaust them first, and you shard only when you have genuinely hit the write-throughput or data-size ceiling of a single optimized, replicated, cached node.

A crucial nuance: the earlier steps mostly scale reads, while sharding is the main way to scale writes. So if your bottleneck is purely read volume, you may never need to shard at all — replicas and cache solve it. Sharding becomes necessary specifically when write throughput or raw data volume exceeds what one node can hold.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India's database is slowing under growth, and an engineer's first instinct is "let us shard." This is exactly the wrong reflex — sharding is the last resort, and the real bottleneck has not been diagnosed.

Problem 2 — Investigation shows the slowness is a missing index plus a read-heavy balance-check load. This is exactly what the first and third steps fix — an index and read replicas, with no sharding needed.

Problem 3 — Only after years of growth does write throughput genuinely exceed one node. This is exactly when sharding is finally justified.

We will build a `ScalingAdvisor` that, given metrics, recommends the next cheapest step in the correct order and explicitly refuses to jump to sharding until the earlier layers are exhausted.

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- The cheapest first step: indexes. Always done before scaling hardware.
CREATE INDEX idx_txn_acct_date ON transactions(account_id, txn_date);

-- Read replica is a DB topology change, not a schema change:
--   (PostgreSQL) configure streaming replication; app routes reads to replica.
-- Sharding is the LAST step and changes the model permanently.
```

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# application.yml
bank:
  scaling:
    max-vertical-cpu: 64        # ceiling of vertical scaling
    read-write-ratio-threshold: 5   # >5:1 reads → replicas/cache help most
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build and run
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/scaling-advisor-1.0.0.jar

# The advisor returns the NEXT correct step given current metrics:
#  unindexed hot query     → OPTIMIZE_QUERIES_INDEXES
#  room on bigger box      → SCALE_UP_VERTICALLY
#  reads >> writes         → ADD_READ_REPLICAS
#  hot data not cached     → ADD_CACHE
#  independent scaling      → APPLY_CQRS
#  writes exceed one node  → SHARD (only now)
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: current database metrics showing a missing index and a five-to-one read-to-write ratio.

Step 1: The advisor receives the metrics. It first checks for unindexed hot queries. It finds one, so it recommends OPTIMIZE_QUERIES_INDEXES — the cheapest step — and stops. No hardware, no sharding.

Step 2: After the index is added, metrics are re-submitted. Now there are no unindexed queries, and the machine still has room to grow, so the advisor recommends SCALE_UP_VERTICALLY.

Step 3: Later, the box is at its core ceiling and the workload is read-heavy at five-to-one. The advisor recommends ADD_READ_REPLICAS to offload reads from the primary.

Step 4: With replicas in place, hot balances are still hitting the database, so the advisor recommends ADD_CACHE.

Step 5: With caching done, the advisor recommends APPLY_CQRS so reads and writes scale independently.

Step 6: Only after all of that, and only when write throughput genuinely exceeds a single node, does the advisor recommend SHARD — and it logs that this is the last resort. At every step the recommendation is the next cheapest action, never a leap to sharding.

```
2026-10-25 13:51:30 INFO  ScalingAdvisor - Fix queries/indexes first — cheapest and often the whole fix.
2026-10-25 13:51:31 INFO  ScalingAdvisor - Read-heavy workload — add read replicas to offload the primary.
2026-10-25 13:51:32 WARN  ScalingAdvisor - All cheaper layers exhausted AND writes exceed one node — shard now.
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  DbMetrics ──→ ScalingAdvisor.recommend()

  cheapest / least disruptive ─────────────────────────→ most / one-way door
  ┌──────────────┐ ┌───────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌───────┐ ┌──────┐ ┌───────┐
  │1 OPTIMIZE    │→│2 SCALE UP │→│3 REPLICAS│→│4 CACHE│→│5 CQRS│→│6 SHARD│
  │ queries/idx  │ │ vertical  │ │ (reads)  │ │(reads)│ │      │ │(last) │
  └──────────────┘ └───────────┘ └──────────┘ └───────┘ └──────┘ └───────┘
       free            no code      offload     µs reads  split    breaks
                       change       primary               r/w      joins+txns

  Advisor returns the FIRST unmet step → never jumps to SHARD early.
  Reads scale via steps 1–4; only SHARD scales WRITES beyond one node.
```

```
  │ OPTIMIZE → SCALE_UP → REPLICAS│
  │ → CACHE → CQRS → SHARD        │
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  Why SHARD is last (guarded by writeThroughputExceedsSingleNode):
    - breaks single-statement joins (fan-out/merge)
    - breaks simple ACID across shards (2PC/saga)
    - breaks auto-increment/global constraints (distributed IDs)
    - bad shard key = hot spots; re-shard moves huge data
    - one-way door: un-sharding is a major project

  Contract for recommend():
    Pre:  current metrics supplied
    Post: returns next cheapest step; SHARD only if all else exhausted + writes exceed node
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The correct order of database scaling steps goes from cheapest and least disruptive to most expensive and most disruptive: first optimize queries and indexes, then scale up vertically, then add read replicas, then add a cache, then apply CQRS, and only then shard. The reason the order matters is that each step is dramatically cheaper and safer than the next, and most systems never need the last step at all.

Optimizing indexes is free in infrastructure terms and is often the entire fix, because a missing index turning a scan into a seek can cut a query a thousandfold. Scaling up vertically needs zero code change and modern hardware gives enormous headroom. Read replicas help because banking workloads are read-heavy, so offloading reads frees the primary for writes. A cache serves hot read-mostly data from memory in microseconds. CQRS then lets the read and write models scale and evolve independently, which is a natural stepping stone.

Sharding is the last resort for concrete reasons. It permanently splits data across nodes, so a join that was a single SQL statement now needs application-side fan-out and merge, transactions that span shards lose simple ACID and need two-phase commit or sagas, auto-increment ids and global constraints stop working so you need distributed id generation, and a bad shard key creates hot spots that are agonizing to fix because re-sharding moves enormous amounts of data. It is effectively a one-way door, and operationally you now run and monitor many nodes each with its own backups and replicas. A key nuance I always add is that the earlier steps mainly scale reads, while sharding is the main way to scale writes, so if the bottleneck is purely read volume you may never need to shard.

At the National Bank of India an engineer wanted to shard the moment the database slowed, but when I diagnosed it, the real causes were a missing index and a read-heavy balance-check load. An index plus read replicas and a cache solved it completely, and we did not shard for years until write throughput genuinely exceeded a single optimized node. The line I always repeat is: optimize, scale up, replicate, cache, apply CQRS, then shard — because sharding is a one-way door that breaks joins and transactions, so I exhaust every cheaper option first.
